speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARIES AND NUMBERS OF JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order in connection with the wording of this resolution. I feel that I should raise the point of order now lest I be told at a later stage of the debate that I should have raised it at this time. I am quite prepared that my point of order should be considered and ruled upon at a later stage, but I would like Your Honour to consider citations 433, 436, 439 and others in Beauchesne, third edition, which have to do with a resolution preceding a money bill.
It seems to me quite clear from these citations that while the resolution preceding a money bill does not need to disclose all the details in the bill, it should set a limit on the amount of money being asked for by the crown. Those citations and others indicate that the debate at the resolution stage is on a certain expenditure asked for by the crown. There is one exception indicated,

which suggests that if no ceiling is placed on the amount, private members may move to increase it when the house is in committee of the whole on the bill. Certainly that is not my purpose in connection with this resolution, but it does seem to me that the government is getting a bit careless in connection with these resolutions and is bringing in too many of them without fixing the maximum amount that may be included in the bill.
Through the years I have made quite a study of this matter, and I have gone over it again in the last day or so. As one goes back through the years it appears that the practice was very well established, until about four or five years ago, that every resolution preceding a money bill spelled out the total amount of money that would be required under that bill. The resolution introduced by the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he was minister of justice, changing the provisions with regard to the pensions of judges so that they could award a portion of their pensions to their widows, spelled out those provisions. So it has been with old age pensions and family allowances. This morning in the library I went back to the records of 1867, 1872 and so on, and down through the years the practice has been very definite. I submit that the government is getting away from the practice of the house and the spirit of the citations to which I have referred when resolutions are brought down in this way.
On a point of privilege I might also express my regret that while the resolution does not tell us the maximum amount involved in this bill, the press seems to have that information. That is another point about which I shall not say more now, but I should like to suggest that by the time this matter reaches another stage we might have consideration by Your Honour as to whether resolutions in this blank cheque form are regular.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECALL OF GENERAL MACARTHUR FROM COMMAND OF UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister of external affairs a question which he may see fit to answer today or at some other time. There seems to be some confusion as to the recall of General MacArthur, arising out of the presidential authority to recall him, in view of the fact that General MacArthur has been the commander of the United Nations forces and we are one of the nations supplying those forces. The question arises whether or not Canada should have been consulted. Would the minister care to make a statement now, or perhaps tomorrow?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECALL OF GENERAL MACARTHUR FROM COMMAND OF UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire at this time, or even tomorrow, to comment on the nature of the action taken by the President of the United States in this matter. I can, however, for the benefit of the hon. member and the house, briefly outline the procedure under which that action was taken.
When the security council, by its resolution of July 7, 1950, established a unified command to conduct the military operations in Korea, it requested the United States to designate the commander of the United Nations forces there. In response to this request of the security council, President Truman the following day designated General MacArthur as the commanding general of the military forces placed by the members of the United Nations under the unified command. I understand that the President of the United States has now decided that the conduct of the military operations in Korea should be entrusted to other hands, and, acting under the mandate given to him by the security council resolution to which I have referred, has appointed General Ridgway as the United Nations commander in place of General MacArthur. This decision is clearly one which falls within the sphere of authority which has been given to the President of the United States by the United Nations itself.
