I should like to read to the house a telegram-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, the member for Quebec-Montmorency.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is fitting that in such an important debate someone should speak in French.
Since I have recently stated my position on the matter under discussion and since I have pointed out my attitude in this respect I will be brief.
I am convinced that steps must be taken at the earliest possible opportunity to stabilize the cost of living and to stem inflation. As a matter of fact, I am afraid it is already too late.
The purchasing power of our dollar has dropped to about 56 cents, and I am convinced
Cost of Living
that this follows the exorbitant profits taken by middlemen, who operate between the producer and the consumer.
Today, more than ever before in the history of our country, big monopolies control, to a large extent, the purchasing power and the distribution of essential goods. Because of their purchasing power, they are in a position to accumulate enormous stocks and control distribution at such times as they feel it will bring them larger profits. Our legislation has enabled those trusts to come into being.
Anyone who takes the trouble to compare the spread between prices paid to producers and those paid by consumers is amazed at the enormous profits made by middlemen.
How can we expect lower costs of production, in poultry farming for instance, when farmers have to pay excessive prices for feed as a result of the operations of the milling trust, exposed in the McGregor report?
During the last war, the government put an embargo on cattle exports to the United States in order to help the British people feed themselves at a reasonable price. To my knowledge, no one objected at the time or claimed that the step might hamper our trade relations with the United States. As controls were also in effect, our people were then able to buy steak, for instance, at a reasonable price.
It is admitted that the higher salaries paid in the United States enable Americans to carry off from our market a large share of the cattle that would normally be sold to Canadian consumers.
During the last war and even afterwards, the government did not hesitate to place an embargo on cattle exports to the United States in order to help feed the British. May I now, sir, request the government to reestablish this embargo or at least to authorize the export of only part of our Canadian cattle. Thus the government would show the Canadian consumers the same consideration it has shown to the British before the embargo was removed and would allow our citizens to make both ends meet.
I realize that this will not please the trusts who, in Canada, control the buying and distributing in this field, but it will surely tend to prevent soulless capitalists from taking advantage of our people.

Cost of Living
I realize that the capitalists who control warehousing in Canada are interested in sustaining the gigantic struggle they are now waging in order to delay as much as possible the setting up of controls, because in the meantime they will be able to store a larger quantity of goods which they will sell at astronomical prices without any danger, since, when the last budget was drafted, it was not deemed advisable to reimpose taxation on surplus profits. Should we always bow to the edicts of higher finance?
For the reasons I have just given and having carefully gone over the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), which reads as follows:
This house is of the opinion that in view of the announcement made on Wednesday last of the greatest monthly increase in Canadian cost of living during the month of February to the disastrously high level of 179-7 points, immediate consideration should be given to the adoption of appropriate measures to hold down the cost of living and halt inflation.
-I have come to the conclusion that I am duty-bound to vote in favour of it, not because I am convinced of the sincerity of the Progressive Conservative party, which has often given proof to this house that it went hand in glove with cartels, but because the amendment, such as it stands, is a true reflection of my opinion and also because I know that the Liberal party respects the opinion of its followers, even though they might occasionally not share the government's own views.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in the debate until the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) interjected some remarks about the high cost of food. The basis of my remarks is taken from yesterday's London Free Press. This quotation that I am going to give you is to point out what a good many people in the country do not realize is going on. Just to be brief, I might say that these figures are taken from the United States department of agriculture's bureau of agricultural economics. The quotation reads as follows:
Like this for example . . . Using last December's prices ... If the farmer gave away the wool in a $50 suit of men's clothing, the suit would still sell for $40.50 ... If he'd give away the wheat in a 16-cent loaf of bread, the loaf would still cost the consumer 13-4 cents ... If the farmer gave away the beans in a 16-cent can of pork and beans, the can would still cost you 14 cents at the grocery store . . . For cigarette smokers . . .
[Mr. LaCroix.l
These are American prices.
... If the tobacco grower gave away the tobacco in a 20-cent pack of cigarettes, the girl behind the counter would still ask you for 17 cents to pay for that purchase.
The impression was left that food prices were too high. That seems to be where everybody wants to bear down with regard to this high cost of living. It is the food prices that they complain about. As I said once before in this house this session, if the people want to eat, they want to be careful what they do when they go to control the prices of various products. The impression has gone abroad that if any controls are put on, the farmer will be the first one to suffer. I think we shall have to decide whether we want to eat anything else besides wheat. We have an abundance of that. But apparently many of the other food products are not going to be in too abundant supply.
I just rose to impress on the house the realization that this forever bearing down on the price of foods and up on other things- and advocating shorter hours-is going to have a final result that we are going to be short of food.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this amendment until I listened to some of the discussion this afternoon. Needless to say, I am going to support this amendment. My chief difficulty, on behalf of many people in this country, is a lack of a parity basis. Certainly we have a runaway inflation to contend with right now. Despite that fact we have some system of controls in this country yet. We have one class of people who have been controlled for some years. We have today a government contract which controls as yet the wheat farmers of this country.
I am not taking any issue with my colleague who has just taken his seat. I agree with everything he has said. I am in hearty agreement with the statement that if we are not careful about this matter there will be a shortage of necessary foodstuffs in this country. I quite agree with all that the hon. member has said. But, Mr. Speaker, under the international wheat agreement we have an extremely unfair set-up. When that agreement was entered into some time ago, it looked as though there might be decreasing wheat values throughout the world as well as in this country. Nobody could foresee the future. The wheat farmers of this country are definitely controlled. They have not any option as to where they may sell their products. The price is set there. Right today the wheat farmer of the prairie provinces is subsidizing the consumers of Canada to the extent of 35 cents a bushel on every

bushel of wheat he delivers and sells. There is there a form of control that the wheat farmer cannot get out from under.
Under this compulsory legislation he is forced to sell his wheat through this government monopoly or set-up we have, and it is not sold on the same basis as it is sold by thfe Americans to the south. Our American neighbour just across the border gets the full value for his wheat. It is true enough-and 1 want to be fair-that they, by virtue of their great population, can handle their wheat situation much more easily than we can handle our great surplus in this country. But over there, while their quota is delivered under the international agreement, the farmer selling the wheat receives the full value for it, the difference between the prevailing value and the price set under the international agreement. The point I want to make is that there was lack of foresight in drawing up that international wheat agreement. There should have been an escalator clause in there whereby-
Why did you not have it put in?
I am not a member of the government.
You were here and did not advocate it at the time.

On another occasion I shall be glad to hear from my hon. friend. I have said that I should like to hear my good friend the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) with regard to this matter. He is one of the best speakers in this House of Commons. I would gladly sit and listen to him expound further on this matter on behalf of the people who sent him here. But I want to say that I think there should be an escalator clause in that international wheat agreement because since it was brought into being farm implements of some types have risen in cost to the farmer by over 60 per cent. Freight rates have increased several times. All this adds to the cost to the farmer producer. While on another occasion I intend to deal much more fully with this international wheat agreement and the hardship that it is going to impose on these wheat producers, I did want to make that point right now, because you do have that matter of control at the present time which, under the present agreement, is going to be the means of creating one of the greatest trimmings that the wheat farmers of the prairie provinces have ever received. You have heard lengthy discussions on other contracts with this country, but I want to make this very clear at this time. The wheat
Cost of Living
farmer right today, according to the market price, is subsidizing the consumers of Canada to the extent of 35 cents a bushel. That is the unfair part of this whole set-up of the government of the day.
I want wholeheartedly to support what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). He said that we have a Combines Investigation Act. That is the law of this country, under which the present government refused to act. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), to whom we have given such great powers in another measure, was the man responsible for pushing the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) around in regard to the investigation of the flour milling industry of this country. That was distinctly costly both to the wheat farmers of this country and to every man, woman and child who consumes bread in Canada. Despite that fact, the Minister of Trade andi Commerce was able to push the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Justice around. The law of the land was then flouted. It was absolutely disregarded by the Minister of Justice who, I think, should have had the intestinal fortitude to stand up to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to the Prime Minister and to his other colleagues and said: Gentlemen, this is my province. I have taken my oath to be responsible for the law of this land, and if I do not carry that out I will be forced to offer you my resignation. I am sorry that the Minister of Justice did not take that attitude. I think he certainly missed the boat to make himself a great national figure in this country, especially when it was just on the eve of a general election. I think it is entirely too bad, and therefore I want wholeheartedly to endorse all that was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre this afternoon. You have certainly a sorry picture in this country when certain businessmen in the east are raising their prices and some branches of the same businesses in the west increase their prices exactly the same amount.
I come back to a point that has been proven in other sessions, namely, that there is something wrong with the processing of many of the farmers' raw materials in this country. The profits to the middlemen are out of all comparison with what the farmer receives for many of his raw materials, and with what the housewife, either of the farmer or of the urban resident, has to pay for the goods she buys. Comparisons have been made year after year along these lines between such places as Minneapolis and Winnipeg, two comparable points. In many instances the farmer in the Minneapolis area

Cost of Living
will receive more lor his product than the farmer in the Winnipeg area. But when they go out to buy the processed article the housewife in the Minneapolis area can buy it cheaper than can the housewife in the Winnipeg area. Something very faulty is going on in this country and it should be thoroughly investigated. We have an act, if our dictator, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, would allow it to operate, to take care of that sort of thing. We have a vicious set-up to contend with, and the government refuses to take action under this measure today.
There is another point that this brings me to, and that is the suggestion made by my very good friend and neighbour, the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith). Like myself, he has been the reeve of a municipality. I am not sure about the provincial acts in Saskatchewan, but he made a suggestion to the government as to how they might assist old age pensioners. I take second place to no hon. member in this house in regard to old age pensioners. My good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has had more to say on behalf of the old age pensioners than any other two or three members in this house. Nevertheless, I am just as much concerned about old age pensioners as any other hon. member of this house. On many occasions I have talked about the plight of the old age pensioners. But my good and personal friend this afternoon made a suggestion that he thought might require an amendment to the British North America Act, to provide additional benefits for the old age pensioners. He suggested that the municipality might bear 25 per cent of the cost of it, if I am correct. I think that is what he suggested, and that the province should bear 25 per cent of the cost and the federal authorities the additional 50 per cent.

Or 5 per
cent.

He did not use the
expression "5 per cent" when he was talking. It is the principle that I want to deal with right here, because we have been through it. Again I come back to the Minister of Justice. When he was premier of Manitoba in 1948 I presume he had an idea that he was coming to Ottawa, but we ordinary citizens of Manitoba had no idea about it at all. As the premier of Manitoba he was concerned about the plight of the old age pensioners, and on behalf of the provincial government he made an offer to the executive of the Manitoba municipal union that until such time as the British North America Act was amended, or appropriate arrangements

were made in the future, the provincial government would bring in enabling legislation by which they could increase the payment for the old age pensioners by $10 a month, and it would be split two ways, $5 by municipalities and $5 by the provincial government, and the municipality would be responsible for the administration and for seeing who should receive it. I think that was the suggestion made by my hon. friend this afternoon.
Well, strange as it may seem-it seemed very strange to me then-the executive of the Manitoba municipal union accepted the offer, which they thought was a fine offer, subject to the approval of the municipal convention, Which was to meet in Winnipeg some weeks later. I have never heard anything argued more fully in detail than that proposition was by the then premier of Manitoba to the municipal officials. After several hours' deliberation and detailed discussion a vote was taken on that offer. And do you know, the result of that vote was approximately 650 against and 7 for, by those municipal officials. I was personally quite happy about it because of this, and this is the point that I do not follow my good friend on. Ever since my experience in municipal life I have been very concerned about increasing the mounting burdens of taxation on real estate. That in itself is creating untold problems and perplexities for municipal corporations throughout Canada, both urban and rural.

I want the
federal government to pay some.

They are called upon to provide many services now. I can cite neighbours of my own in my own constituency who, through no fault of their own, have lost a crop or revenue from some of the best land in that constituency for the eighth year now. It is the most highly assessed farm property in that area. They are called upon to pay increasing taxation whether any revenue comes off the property or not. It is that matter of principle that I want to deal with, and take issue with my good friend from Moose Mountain on.. As long as I am in public life in any capacity I hope I shall fight to overcome that undue burden which is being imposed on real estate, causing so many difficulties in so many municipalities of this country.
While I am on my feet I want again to reiterate my concern for the welfare of the old age pensioners in this country. I know many of these people personally, and I do not know how they obtain the necessities of life these days under the allowances that they are paid. They do have a great hardship. Rather than the suggestion made by

my good friend this afternoon, I think there is a good deal more logic in the resolution placed on the order paper by my colleague the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). I think there is real meat in that resolution, and I hope it is discussed in the house and that we shall have an opportunity to express our views to the government on that resolution.
I think it is most important that worthwhile measures be taken to assist those old age pensioners and many other pensioners throughout the country who are finding it so very difficult. As I said, I had not intended to discuss this matter, but in municipal life or in the federal picture or anywhere else I have not missed an opportunity to set forth the problems confronting the municipal corporations in this country, both urban and rural; and I hope that no legislation is ever put forward by this federal government or by provincial governments which will add to that unfair proposition, of increasing taxation on real estate, those social services which do not entirely belong to the municipalities. I want to make that point very clear. I shall have much more to say about the international wheat agreement at another time. However, I cite that as one example of controls by the government-and very unfair controls-where the wheat producer has no alternative. He is now subsidizing the consumer in Canada. As I have said, he is subsidizing the consumer to the extent of 35 cents a bushel, right today. His problems are increasing from day to day, because his costs of production are increasing in many respects.
Anyone who lives in the prairie provinces, whether he be a city dweller or not, must realize these facts fully. Therefore I think there must be some system of parity granted in Canada during these difficult days of inflation and increasing living costs. I shall certainly support the amendment. I believe it is most timely, and in the interests of the consumer in this country, especially the parents who find it so difficult, in some instances because of frozen incomes, to provide for their families today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on this subject. I know many members are desirous of winding up the debate; but, so far as I am concerned, I am not particularly anxious to wind it up because I think this is unfinished business since 1945. Unless we settle it somewhere it seems to me we will just have a repetition of what is going on now.
One would judge, from the attitude of the government, that they have made up their
Cost of Living
minds that there are to be no price controls, as such, at this time.
Hear, hear.

Someone says "hear, hear". Well, I consider this the most important debate we have had for a long time, because the cost of living is one of the most disturbing factors in the country.
It is all right to talk about defence, and all that kind of thing. We realize it is necessary to make preparations for defence; but do not let us forget that our main weapon of defence is the people who will produce the wherewithal for defence, and pay the taxes that will provide the weapons. That must be considered also.
The representatives of the organized labour movement in Canada represent a large portion of the industrial workers in this country. They have made their wishes known on many occasions. Only very recently joint representations were made by the Trades and Labour Congress, the Canadian Congress of Labour and the Catholic Federation. In their submission to the government they pointed out in no uncertain terms they thought the time had come when the government should take at least some action to give some indication that the cost of living is going to be held somewhere.
The government has not done this. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has made it clear that, so far as he is concerned, he is speaking for the government and that no action to prevent inflation is going to take place at this time in connection with a system of price controls. I say that an answer of that kind to the representatives of the people who work in the mines and the factories which produce the means for defence, and supply a great portion of the taxation to pay for defence equipment, is an unrealistic answer.
While the cost of living statistics may not be as accurate as they could or should be, nevertheless they are an indication of what the cost of living actually is. I say that the figure 179-7, as the over-all cost of living index, does not reflect actually what is being imposed upon the average citizen. We get some idea what the average person maintaining a home is up against when we take the food index figure of 233-9, because 80 per cent of the money spent in the home of the person in the average income group is spent for food. That is the figure that should be used.
People see the cost of living climbing from day to day, and the stand has been taken by the government that nothing is going to

Cost of Living
be done. This is discouraging. It amuses me to hear hon. members say that they do not want price controls, because if they would stop and think they would realize they have price fixing now, in respect of nearly every commodity entering their homes. However, that price fixing is done by people who are not responsible to the Canadian people generally or to the House of Commons. Large corporations across this country do not ask the permission of anyone when they want to step up a price.
For instance, take a look at the recent price increase in new automobiles. That increase certainly was not warranted by the 5 per cent tax imposed by the government last September. But prices have skyrocketed, whether we like it or not. Then we see overnight an artificial shortage of butter, and overnight 15 or 20 cents per pound is added to the price. Who is fixing that price? It is very definitely fixed.
We see irresponsible price fixing right across the country today in connection with practically every commodity one is compelled to buy.
We are asking for a system of responsible controls, and we are prepared to have the Canadian government institute the machinery which would be responsible to parliament in connection with the fixing of prices in this time of stress and concern. This process of getting all the traffic will bear and supporting the system of price fixing we now have is certainly not my understanding of a proper system of responsible government for the Canadian people.
Let me emphasize that hon. members who say they do not want price controls, that they are hard to administer and all that sort of thing, must balance that argument against the argument that prices are already fixed in practically every commodity. It is a matter of determining whether we will continue that kind of system which can create overnight artificial shortages and bring about a skyrocketing of prices, without consultation with anybody, or whether we want to hand the problem over to the government so that it may be handled as it was handled during the war-and very successfully.
That is what we have to ascertain. Apparently the government has not faced up to the question.
On motion of Mr. Gillis the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
For tomorrow consideration had been given to the possibility of dealing with the estimates of the Department of National Defence-both tomorrow

and Friday. But, on considering the matter, it has been found that that would not be convenient for hon. members of the house, and that more than a few hours' notice would be required before opening a discussion on the estimates of the defence department.
In view of that I think it would probably suit the convenience of hon. members if we continued and tried to complete the debate which stands as the first order on the order paper, the present debate on the motion that Mr. Speaker leave the chair, notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 28 that on Thursdays and Fridays Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair to go into committee of supply, without question put. If I had the unanimous consent of the house I would move that on Thursday, tomorrow, and Friday, the next day, if necessary, standing order 28 be suspended so that the debate on government order No. 1 on today's order paper may be first concluded and four additional departments called for the first time, not for the purpose of proceeding with them but for the purpose of having them before the committee as would happen on the conclusion of this debate, and then to proceed with the estimates of the Department of Transport.
Thursday and Friday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The first thing we would do would be to try to complete this debate on the motion of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), as leader of the house, to go into committee of supply and the amendment of the leader of the opposition. That debate being concluded, unless there were further discussions before the motion could be put to go into committee of supply, upon that motion being resolved the four additional departments that were mentioned originally for Monday would first be called and the items allowed to stand. Then we would proceed with the estimates of the Department of Transport.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether the transport estimates are to be considered on both Thursday and Friday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If we got along rapidly enough, the idea would be to do something more on Friday, and we would announce Thursday night what it would be. I would imagine that we would take all of tomorrow to conclude this debate and the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Transport. If they were not concluded we would continue with them on Friday, and announce either the estimates of the Department of Fisheries or the Department of Agriculture to follow the completion of the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Transport.

The effect of this motion of course would be spent when the question of going into supply on the motion made on Monday was resolved.

Mr. Speaker, I will support the suggestion of the Prime Minister. In view of the nature of the debate now taking place, it would seem satisfactory to me that it should proceed to a conclusion. Under the circumstances it would seem obvious that adequate notice should be given with respect to the opening of the Department of National Defence in view of the number of hon. members who are anxious to deal with that very important subject. I would hope that unanimous consent would be given to the motion made by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on this proposal. I want to say that I am a reasonable person, and certainly I am ready to agree with respect to a part of what the Prime Minister suggests. As to another part of it, however, he has not yet convinced me. It could be argued that it is desirable that the present debate should be continued tomorrow. The part of the Prime Minister's request that I accept is that unanimous consent be given to suspending the rule so that the debate may be carried on on Thursday and Friday, which is otherwise irregular. Then he goes on and asks that when we get into committee of supply the four departments which were named for last Monday should be opened. I am not just being stubborn about this. The fact of the matter is that this is one of the few but very important provisions in the rules of the house whereby private members of parliament can bring their views as effectively as they can to the attention of the government. We do it not only by our speeches but also by the fact that we hold more or less of a whiphand with respect to getting into committee of supply, where money is voted. Before the Prime Minister rises to his feet, I am going to suggest that we reach a compromise. I will give unanimous consent to the first part of his suggestion but not to the calling of four departments. How about compromising on two?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Why should it be only two? The motion was made for the purpose of going into committee of supply and calling four departments. It has been debated, and it will have been as fully debated as any motion to go into committee of supply that I can remember in the several sessions that I have been here. It would seem to me that there would be no serious inconvenience in that because there will not be another opportunity of opening departments next week. We expect the debate on the budget to proceed next week. Of all the departments there are
Business of the House
only four that have been placed before the committee of supply up to this time. I do not think that hon. members would be forgoing any right because normally when this motion is disposed of four departments would be called. If it is preferable to dispose of it on Thursday or Friday we would like to do so if it will not prevent it from having the same effect as if it were disposed of on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Prime Minister says that normally the effect of this motion would have been to get into committee of supply and open four departments. Normally such a motion could not be disposed of except on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. Therefore since the house has debated it up until this time, normally-in other words, without unanimous consent-it cannot be proceeded with again until another Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. I suggest that, since the Prime Minister is asking us to give unanimous consent to upsetting that part of the rule, he should compromise on the other part. I have met him more than halfway, and some of my friends over here think I have gone too far.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Some of my friends think I have gone too far, and that I should not have suggested' that we continue this debate. I thought it would be convenient for most members if it were continued. If it is the desire of the house that we abide by the rule, I will not submit the motion. If it cannot have the same effect as if it were disposed' of on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, let us wait for a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday to dispose of it.
I should like to add that the next time a motion is made to go into committee of supply we should not have in mind four departments. One is quite sufficient.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the hon. member becomes the leader of the house he will determine any announcements of what he will ask the house to do. We announced that we were going to ask to go into committee of supply and open four departments.
Mr. Speaker, this happens to be one case in which the Prime Minister will bow to the will of the opposition.

He will not bow to the
will of the opposition but will conform to the rules of the house.
